newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition boycotts Yugoslav parliament.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition boycotts Yugoslav parliament.

text.p: Serbian opposition parties boycotted the Yugoslav federal parliament on Tuesday, vowing to stay away until Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic admitted he cheated them of local election victories last month.

Their boycott of the first post-election session of parliament came as NATO foreign ministers meeting in Brussels called on Milosevic to revoke the cancellation of municipal poll results which the opposition said it had won.

The first round of the municipal poll was held on November 3, the same day federal elections were held in which Milosevic's ruling socialists and their allies came close to a two-thirds majority in the parliament of Yugoslavia, which comprises Serbia and Montenegro.
In the Serbian municipal polls, the opposition Zajedna (Together) coalition claimed victory in Belgrade and 14 other towns.

Milosevic's socialists, determined to preserve the total power they have wielded for 50 years, used the courts to overturn the local poll results, prompting a wave of street demonstrations in Belgrade and other disputed towns calling for the ousting of the Serbian leader.
Although the opposition did not contest the legitimacy of the federal vote, Zajedno leader Zoran Djindjic said:
"Zajedno's 22 deputies will boycott all sessions of the federal parliament until the results of the (municipal) elections are recognised."

The federal election results gave the Serbian socialists, their leftist coalition partners and their Montenegrin allies 84 of the 138 seats, just six short of a two-thirds majority which would allow Milosevic to change the constitution.
Political sources said Milosevic would not find it hard to muster the votes he needed among the smaller parties to force through constitutional change to keep him in power.
His term as Serbian president expires next year and there has been speculation he could become federal president after turning it into an executive post modelled on France's powerful presidency.
The running conflict over the municipal election has upset this scenario, severely denting Milosevic's electoral credibility ahead of Serbian republic elections which must be held next year.

The legality of the results is currently under examination by the federal supreme court after the Serbian supreme court rejected opposition appeals at the weekend, giving a fresh head of steam to Zajedno street rallies mobilising up to 150,000 people a day.
The U.S. and other Western governments have supported the opposition, backing their demands for socialist recognition of Zajedno's win with threats of reprisals.
Tuesday's NATO statement praised the opposition for ensuring its demonstrations were peaceful.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, in Brussels for the NATO meeting, warned that if Milosevic wanted to "rule Serbia as an unreformed dictatorship, it will only increase his isolation and the suffering of his people."
The remark was read as a clear hint that Washington would back the reimposition of U.N. sanctions imposed on Yugoslavia for 3-1/2 years during the war in Bosnia.
The Serbian economy is still in ruins from the last round of sanctions which mothballed industries that Milosevic has no money to revive.
Yugoslavia is denied entry to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank and Washington is expected to veto its membership even if Milosevic meets the bodies' terms.
But the case for sanctions is far from clearcut and Zajedno has been signalling to the West that it would oppose them.

Independent economist Zoran Popov told Reuters on Tuesday that Milosevic could survive for a year or two with a siege economy, barter deals with Russia and China and hard currency savings still held by Serbs.
"That way, we could still manage to increase output by some seven percent next year, albeit from a very low base," he added. "This can't go on forever but for a very long time."
